sources.title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench (AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe keynote)
sources.note: Local machine transcript (faster-whisper), no speaker labels, Dex alone; names mishear (Astra, Sol, Fable are model names as transcribed). Full text read.

sources.title: Beyond Coding ep. 270: Why Coding Agents Keep Making Your Codebase Worse
sources.note: Local machine transcript, no speaker labels; host Patrick Akil's turns not carded; attributed to Dex by content. Full text read.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: unattended, models will not improve or maintain your code-based quality over time
cards.claim: Core thesis: models left unattended do not improve or even maintain codebase quality, so a no-review (lights-out) factory is premature.
cards.evidence_detail: Backed by SlopCodeBench and the May report, but stated as thesis.
cards.landing: Keep refuter/reviewer stage; do not drop human review of maintainability.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: maintainability has no fast oracle
cards.claim: RL and verifiers need a fast oracle, but maintainability is only discovered months later, so models are not trained against it.
cards.landing: Rationale for why verifier scripts cannot replace a human on architecture.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: GPT 5.5 was the best model on the market. It got a 14.8%.
cards.claim: SlopCodeBench (multi-checkpoint, evolving-feature benchmark from a Wisconsin lab) scored the best model 14.8% at launch, against 95% on saturated benchmarks.
cards.evidence_detail: 14.8% GPT 5.5 at launch; contrasted with ~95% terminal-bench-type scores.
cards.landing: Evidence base for treating verifier quality, not model choice, as the lever.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Astra is 1.5% percentage points higher than GPD 5.5.
cards.claim: Newest model gains only about 1.5 points on SlopCodeBench over GPT 5.5, so maintainability improves slower than claimed.
cards.landing: Do not assume next model fixes quality; matches 'do not mortgage' rule.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: that'll be GPT-7's problem. Folks, we're at GPT6
cards.claim: Changes the earlier 'sloppy now, next model fixes it' stance: models got better at computer use and demos but not at code-quality, so he stops betting on future models.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites online reports and benchmark; no numbers beyond SlopCodeBench.
cards.landing: Supports reading code now; informs W1/W4 decision not to wait for models.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: since January ... code review quality is way down
cards.claim: Cites a May report that since Opus 4.5 adoption review quality fell, more PRs skip review, incidents per PR and bugs per developer rose, and he rejects 'skill issue'.
cards.evidence_detail: Third-party report cited, no figures given in talk.
cards.landing: Argument for keeping review gates and PR-bound reviewer.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: for now we should probably read the code
cards.claim: Because unattended output degrades, the engineer should read the code; his 12-factor-factories list starts from that.
cards.landing: Owner-read step in closing message / owner view.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Plan before you build. 20 minutes, 30 minutes up front, can save you hours
cards.claim: Factor one: 20-30 minutes of planning before building saves hours in review, as teams did before AI.
cards.landing: Phase routine plan phase (Plan @ sha).

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Don't overplan, though.
cards.claim: Plan depth is an expected-pain curve: a two-sentence prompt has ~50% rework chance, a five-hour hand-written spec ~10%, hand-writing 0%; tune per task by how likely and how painful the change is.
cards.landing: Gate on plan depth by task risk instead of one routine for all.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Find ways to let the model give you information in a way that doesn't make you have to read walls
cards.claim: Align visually: a 'show me' skill (open source, ~20K installs) has the model present plans, stacked-PR breakdown and order of changes visually rather than as prose.
cards.landing: Skill candidate; owner one-page view.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Give them a browser, let them run the app, let them use curl, let them record videos.
cards.claim: Help agents test their own work with browser, running app, curl and video, as backpressure.
cards.landing: Verifier tooling for web/mobile slices.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: There's about 100 anti-slop rules.
cards.claim: Points to a third-party catalogue of ~100 Oxlint rules for agent anti-patterns in TypeScript, plus rules in the SlopCodeBench paper, as steal-able deterministic backpressure.
cards.evidence_detail: ~100 rules; repo by Dylan Milroy as transcribed.
cards.landing: Custom ESLint rules in web/mobile CI; Ruff rules for backend.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: have the pager alert come with the PR the agent thinks will fix it
cards.claim: Feed incidents and support tickets into the factory: the alert arrives with an agent-drafted fix PR, even if only half are mergeable.
cards.landing: Sentry-to-PR workflow idea for the ops console.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: loops are basically a combination of forward pressure and back pressure
cards.claim: Demystifies 'loops': triggers that start work (schedules, webhooks) plus feedback while working so the agent hill-climbs without a human.
cards.landing: Framing for workflow library: trigger plus backpressure.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: go analyze the sessions of your team, figure out what they're struggling with
cards.claim: Compound over time: analyze team sessions for struggles and feed them into skills or memory.
cards.landing: Transcript review feeding skills; helps distinguish skipped routine from unused store.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: sessions and plans and prompts and all this stuff kind of lives in a centralized
cards.claim: The AI-native forge needs a central system of record for sessions, plans and prompts, instead of pasting between chats; diffs stream to the cloud so review need not wait for PRs.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha PR body and journal as the interim record.

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: even Steve's come around
cards.claim: Cites Steve Yegge's reversal (after a year of 'read code and fall behind') that models write unreadable complexity they cannot debug, as support for reading code.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.source_title: State of Software Factories // Slop Bench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Let models experiment, give them feature flagging tooling
cards.claim: Back pressure for UI: ship several variants behind flags and let user behaviour pick, since models cannot see UI as humans do.
cards.landing: Low relevance to single-tenant shop app; mobile UI verification idea.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: do not mortgage your code base
cards.claim: Do not accept sloppy code hoping a future model will fix it; labs hill-climb other things and the last 10% of maintainability may be as hard as the first 90%.
cards.landing: Standing rule for reviewer: no deferring structural debt to future models.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it gives the model a thing to build, Greenfield. And then it says, cool, now take that code base
cards.claim: SlopCodeBench differs from SWE-bench-style, marathon and judge-model benchmarks by evolving one codebase over 3-10 checkpoints without disclosing the whole problem; failing tests trend up for all models.
cards.evidence_detail: 3-10 checkpoints per challenge; GPT 5.5 about 15% in May, newest model 16.5% (his sponsored run).
cards.landing: Design verifiers around evolution across tasks, not one-shot tests.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: from 25,000 foot view ... eliminate like 50% of the bad things
cards.claim: Planning in zoom levels (one-pager, then design) eliminates about 50% then 80% of bad solutions, aiming for 0-10% rework versus 25-55% when one-shotting large agent PRs; the code, not the spec, stays source of truth.
cards.evidence_detail: Estimated percentages 50%, 80%, 0-10% vs 25-55% rework; not measured.
cards.landing: Plan phase structure: one-page first, design second.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we call it a design doc rather than a plan
cards.claim: A design doc separates end state from how to get there; teams customize it, e.g. four required questions at the top, and conventions vary per team.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha body template with required top questions.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: plenty of teams where Fable has just been banned.
cards.claim: Some enterprise teams ban the most expensive model by default and require a request for temporary access per task, as a model-spend control.
cards.landing: Effort/model routing default with justified escalation.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: give the model better steering and skills of like, hey, here's how to keep it concise
cards.claim: PM-written 10-page AI documents were rejected as slop and detached from the code; fix with concision skills plus a pipeline that researches all repos, then interrogates the author (grill-me style) on problem and success measure.
cards.landing: Skill pairing: concise-writing skill plus interrogation step before specs.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I think most of it is BS.
cards.claim: Dark-factory claims from executives are mostly posturing; a principal-engineer example shows 30,000-line slop PRs where 90% AI-written claims are made.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: figure out how to go two to three times faster.
cards.claim: Aim for 2-4x incrementally and compound, not 10x-100x by discarding all engineering practice.
cards.landing: Expectation setting for adoption of routine/workflow library.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: culture beats process every single time
cards.claim: On dropping pull requests: ownership culture (author owns it alone, no shared blame with reviewer) matters more than PR process; but he sends design docs to the CTO early because fixing before merge is cheaper.
cards.landing: Early plan-review step; owner is author of record.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I have never seen a prompt or a deterministic tool that can like drive code base maintainability
cards.claim: Screenshots and videos show correctness only; linters and cyclomatic-complexity limits block categories of slop, but nothing deterministic or prompted drives maintainability without a human in the loop.
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts as floor; reviewer/human remains for architecture.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the thing that makes that skill useful is is having a human in the loop
cards.claim: Uses Matt Pocock's improve-codebase-architecture skill, sometimes accepting first fixes unseen, but its value comes from a human steering the refactor direction.
cards.landing: Candidate skill for the 13-package set.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The worst pull request comment is like this is wrong I rewrote it for you
cards.claim: Good review comments probe and point to existing patterns; but pasting comments to an AI means the author learns nothing, so design-doc review becomes the place to coach prompting.
cards.evidence_detail: Observations; Hashimoto 'ask your Claude why' example relayed.
cards.landing: Reviewer comments that point to repo patterns rather than rewrite.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: design doc is basically a prompt
cards.claim: Because a design doc is a prompt, commenting on it teaches the author better prompting and may become as important as code review.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha PR as reviewable prompt.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: at least 50 to 60% of our work is like basically one-shotted
cards.claim: His team's mix: 50-60% small one-shot changes (under a couple hundred lines) with no up-front planning, ~10% of PRs from overnight janitor bots, ~30% via the research-plan-implement family.
cards.landing: Tier the routine: skip plan phase for small changes.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: It's kind of like a thermostat, right?
cards.claim: Janitor bots hold a desired end state (refactors, lint-rule fixes, migrations) via small nightly PRs, at most one open per PR type tracked by labels, and no new run until the last is merged (kanban limit).
cards.landing: Scheduled workflow candidate with WIP limit by label.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If the PR is too big, it never gets merged.
cards.claim: Automated PRs must be small and digestible.
cards.landing: Size cap on agent PRs.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: another session that doesn't know what the ticket was
cards.claim: Research is run in a session that does not know the ticket so it stays objective, then plan sessions (product requirements first if ambiguous, then design, then an ordering doc).
cards.evidence_detail: Own process; acronym garbled by transcription.
cards.landing: Research phase with blind brief; one phase per session.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's a lot easier to ship 10,000 lines of code if you check it every thousand lines
cards.claim: Large work is broken into checkpointed chunks (about every 1,000 lines), sometimes as stacked PRs, to shrink the debug surface.
cards.landing: Ordering doc plus stacked PR per checkpoint.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I use Soul for almost everything now.
cards.claim: Parent and subagent model pairings are chosen per task (big orchestrating small, or same model), he uses one model for nearly everything, and cross-provider orchestration needs the Codex CLI for now.
cards.evidence_detail: Model names as transcribed (Soul, Fable, Opus).
cards.landing: Model routing per agent definition.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: do not send anyone code for review that you yourself have not read
cards.claim: Internal cultural rule: read your agent's code before sending it for review; he sometimes changes half of it or throws it out and returns to design.
cards.landing: Closing-message question: did the author read the diff.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can just throw out the output and try again
cards.claim: Incremental zoom-in planning (product, tech, steps) lets you discard output and return to an earlier level at any point.
cards.landing: Allow phase rollback to design instead of patching.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: do less things in parallel
cards.claim: Fewer concurrent tasks give faster end-to-end value; plan two things, watch them, always keep one most important thing that wins when unblocked; do not wake to 10,000 lines overnight.
cards.evidence_detail: No measurements; he says he wants a study.
cards.landing: WIP limit on parallel phases/PRs.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm willing to, like, async for 15, 20 minutes
cards.claim: A 10-20 minute async research step in a large repo gives the model 90-99% of needed context and misses are easy to find, which beats steering it interactively.
cards.landing: Research phase as a separate async session producing a doc.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: no enterprise has subscription plans. They're all paying per token.
cards.claim: Token-maxing on subscriptions does not transfer to serious work; enterprises pay per token for security and retention, so spend discipline (L1) matters and 'skill issue' is not 'too few tokens'.
cards.evidence_detail: Customers with 15 engineers on per-token plans.
cards.landing: Cost-aware effort routing for verifiers.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We haven't figured out how to put that taste into models.
cards.claim: Architectural taste comes from being bitten over years; models lack it, so humans must supply it, and juniors need mentorship by probing questions to build it.
cards.evidence_detail: No data; relays a peer's plea for deletion/refactor RL tasks.
cards.landing: Encode owner's architectural rules as reviewer checklist items.

gaps: Keynote is cut short on details: no numbers for the May report, and 'show me' skill and the anti-slop rule repo are named only in passing.
Machine transcripts misspell model names (Astra, Sol, Fable) and the RPI successor acronym; names in cards follow the transcript.
Podcast host turns not carded; the 'Instagram phase' phrase belongs to a third party.
